header.incumbent: Braintree (inferred, not stated: the incumbent's account-manager churn and the saved-card and PayPal/Venmo 'what do we lose' questions point to it)
header.tag_why: The deal moved from bake-off to 'when' only after a customer engineer built a working sitter payment flow in our sandbox over a weekend, and marketplace onboarding and local-currency payouts were the fit that made that prototype matter.

evidence.excerpt: Expansion. They were launching Canada, then the UK, and sitters have to get paid locally.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: a haunted house.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Two engineers more or less full-time just keeping sitter payments working.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: There was also a roadmap item, faster pay for sitters, that had been pushed three quarters in a row.
evidence.label: fact

trigger.insight: Expansion was the deadline, but the real pain was engineering toil: two engineers babysitting sitter pay while the faster-sitter-pay roadmap item slipped three quarters. That is a ready-made cost-of-doing-nothing case, and nobody turned it into a business case. Our M1 'grow globally, in every currency' only touches the expansion half and misses the toil half that Daniel kept repeating.
trigger.messaging: Lead with reclaiming the engineers and shipping faster sitter pay ('payments shouldn't be a team'), and use M1's global reach as the reason it holds up in Canada and the UK.

evidence.excerpt: Daniel. He signed.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: this is an engineering decision, finance will sign what I bring them.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: The CFO joined one call for ten minutes, asked one question,
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: does this change when sitters get paid?
evidence.label: quote

decider.insight: This was an engineering-owned buy. Daniel told the rep the rules early and the deal followed them, so the buyer persona is the VP of Engineering. Finance cared about exactly one thing, sitter pay timing, which is the same promise as 'paid by Friday'. The transcript never says what answer the CFO got.
decider.messaging: Pitch marketplace deals like this to the engineering leader, and give finance a one-line answer on sitter pay timing ('sitters still get paid by Friday, or sooner').

evidence.excerpt: I've stopped learning their names.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: A lot of pet owners pay with PayPal and Venmo, and they were nervous about what happens to those buttons.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: It went from "how fast can we build this" to "what do we lose."
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I assume Braintree told them they'd lose things. I don't know that. That's me guessing.
evidence.label: opinion

competitor.insight: The incumbent's weakness was relationship churn, not product, and our M5 answers it with tiered response times instead of named people. The incumbent's defense was fear of loss: after the Braintree call, the questions turned to PayPal, Venmo and saved cards. That shift is observed; what Braintree actually said is the rep's guess. Whatever was said, 'what do we lose' was the incumbent's strongest ground, and we had no prepared answer for it.
competitor.messaging: Pre-empt 'what do we lose' with an explicit answer on PayPal, Venmo and saved-card migration, and replace tiered-SLA language with a named owner who stays.

evidence.excerpt: Reaction: the docs and the sandbox.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: One of their engineers, on her own time, built a working sitter payment flow over a weekend and showed it at Monday standup.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: And the marketplace piece. Onboarding sitters, the identity checks, paying out in local currency.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: our average booking is 38 dollars, I'm not losing sleep over auth rates.
evidence.label: quote

message.insight: M2 won because the customer experienced it, not because we claimed it; the rep didn't even know the prototype existed. M11 landed on substance, though the customer didn't use our words for it. M4 died on contact: a generic 'average uplift' means nothing to a $38-ticket business whose pain is paying sitters, not authorizing owners.
message.messaging: For low-ticket marketplaces, drop the acceptance-rate slide and replace it with a sandbox invitation: build sitter pay with local-currency payouts in a weekend.

evidence.excerpt: The weekend prototype. Before that it was a bake-off. After that Daniel stopped saying "if."
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I didn't even know until Daniel told me.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Only that I barely sold this. Their engineer did.
evidence.label: opinion

decided.insight: The turning point was something we didn't plan and didn't see coming: an unprompted customer engineer proving 'how fast can we build this' for herself. That makes the win repeatable only if the hands-on build becomes a deliberate step. It also shows Daniel's 'engineering decision' was really made by his engineers.
decided.messaging: Make 'your engineer builds it in a weekend' an explicit proof point and offer the sandbox build early in engineering-led deals, rather than waiting for it to happen.

evidence.excerpt: Nothing, really. It was a clean one.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: I didn't have a crisp answer on Venmo in the room, and I still don't.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: who's done this at our size without losing cards?
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: we'll find out.
evidence.label: quote

gaps.insight: It was not a clean deal: PayPal was deferred to implementation, Venmo is still unanswered, and Daniel's request for a same-size saved-card migration reference was never fulfilled. All of this carried into kickoff as 'we'll find out'. The win rode on prototype momentum and handed the risk to implementation; 'they decided it was a risk they'd take' is the rep's read, not the customer's words.
gaps.messaging: We need a named customer story about migrating saved cards at comparable scale without losing any (M8 is too generic), plus a one-line answer on keeping PayPal and Venmo.

evidence.excerpt: Payments shouldn't be a team,
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: We want to stop babysitting this.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: On the sitter side it's "paid by Friday." The whole promise to sitters is paid by Friday.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: And nobody says "payouts." They say "sitter pay."
evidence.label: fact

language.insight: They describe the problem as toil ('haunted house', 'babysitting', 'shouldn't be a team') and as a promise to sitters ('paid by Friday'). Our vocabulary of 'marketplace', 'payouts' and 'authorization rates' isn't theirs; they say 'the app' and 'sitter pay'. 'Paid by Friday' is also exactly what the CFO asked about, so it is the phrase both buyers share.
language.messaging: Rewrite M11 for gig and service apps in their words, for example: 'Pay your people by Friday, in every country, without a payments team.'

gaps.question: What was the answer on keeping Venmo (and PayPal) after the switch?
gaps.follow_up: Ask product/solutions engineering for a definitive answer on PayPal and Venmo support, then have Priya send it to Daniel before implementation reaches checkout.

gaps.question: Who has migrated saved cards at Fetchwell's size without losing any?
gaps.follow_up: Ask customer success for a comparable migration reference, deliver it to Daniel, and ask Daniel's engineer after migration how many cards came over cleanly.

gaps.question: What did Braintree actually tell them on the mid-evaluation call?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Daniel directly what Braintree said they would lose by switching.

gaps.question: What answer did the CFO get to 'does this change when sitters get paid?'
gaps.follow_up: Ask Priya what was said in response, and ask Daniel whether sitter pay timing changes after go-live.

gaps.question: What did they ask for that we couldn't show?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Priya to list every open item from the evaluation (PayPal, Venmo, card reference, anything else) and who owns each in implementation.

gaps.question: Was the cost of two engineers on sitter payments or the delayed faster-pay item ever quantified with the customer?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Priya whether Daniel put a number on it, and ask Daniel at the 90-day check-in what the engineers were moved to.

close.rep_takeaway: Priya's candor that she 'barely sold this' is the most useful thing in this review: the deal turned when a customer engineer got hands-on in the sandbox. Next time, put the sandbox in an engineer's hands on purpose, early. Also, a deal isn't 'clean' when there's an unanswered 'who's done this at our size?' and no Venmo answer. Close those loops before signature, or they turn up at kickoff as 'we'll find out'.
